input: Ask neighbors to form a street emergency plan

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: The plan's depth and content changes drastically depending on whether this covers basic contact sharing, evacuation routes, resource pooling, or a full multi-hazard response protocol.
The approach differs significantly based on how many households are involved and whether any key neighbors are already on board or need to be persuaded from scratch.
The type of emergencies most relevant to plan for (wildfires, earthquakes, floods, power outages) depends on the local geography and risk environment.
Time availability shapes whether this is a one-meeting effort or a multi-week project, and budget affects whether printed materials, a shared app, or a hosted event is feasible.
The immediate next action — whether to knock on doors, send a group message, post a flyer, or call a meeting — depends on how neighbors currently communicate.
Some people want a formal written plan with roles assigned; others prefer a loose agreement. The tone of outreach (official/serious vs. friendly/casual) also affects buy-in.
Knowing what 'done' looks like — a signed document, a group chat, a held meeting, or a practiced drill — determines how far the planning needs to go.

gold.taskTitle: Get Neighbors to Form a Street Emergency Plan
gold.taskDescription: Coordinate with neighbors to create a shared emergency preparedness plan for the street or immediate community.

questions.title: What specific emergencies should the plan cover?
questions.description: Identify the primary hazards to plan for — e.g., power outages, wildfires, earthquakes, floods — to scope the plan's content appropriately.

questions.title: How many households are you trying to include?
questions.description: Determine the scale of the effort — a few immediate neighbors vs. the entire street — as this shapes coordination complexity.

questions.title: What should the plan actually contain at minimum?
questions.description: Clarify whether the goal is a shared contact list, assigned roles, evacuation routes, stockpiled supplies, or a combination.

questions.title: How do neighbors currently communicate with each other?
questions.description: Identify the existing channel — in person, group chat, Nextdoor, email list — to determine the best outreach method.

questions.title: How much time can you dedicate to organizing this?
questions.description: Understand the time and budget constraints to decide whether this is a quick one-meeting effort or a structured multi-step project.

questions.title: Should the tone be formal and official or casual and friendly?
questions.description: Determine the communication style for outreach and the plan itself, since this affects neighbor buy-in and the format of materials.

questions.title: What would make this effort feel complete and successful to you?
questions.description: Define the end goal — a held meeting, a written document, a group chat, a completed drill — so the plan has a clear finish line.
